scenes.source: README Part 1 intro; source-facts.md (how the recording was made)
scenes.narration: A quick note on what this chapter is. It shows one example pipeline running on a throwaway Jenkins on this machine. The screens are real screenshots, and the terminal output is replayed from real runs. To make the recording, the two credentials, the job and the approval were sent through Jenkins web interface, instead of being clicked by hand. One clip is different: a live recording of the same pipeline, made separately, where the approval is typed in by hand. Nothing is converted here. That comes in later chapters.
onScreen: One example pipeline on a disposable local Jenkins
Real screenshots and replayed terminal output
Credentials, job and approval were sent by script, not clicked
Plus one live recording, made separately, approved by hand
Not shown here: any conversion to GitHub Actions

data.foot: The aim: know exactly what the pipeline does, so later chapters can check the copy against it.

scenes.narration: The example is a small stock-keeping service called inventory service. Its Jenkinsfile, the script that tells Jenkins what to do, builds it, tests it, packages it, publishes it and deploys it. It takes three settings: a release version, a deployment environment, and whether to run the integration tests. It also needs two secrets.

onScreen.v: inventory-service, a small Python stock-keeping tool
A Jenkinsfile: build, test, package, publish, deploy
Release version, deploy environment, run integration tests
A repository login and a deployment token

scenes.narration: The stages run in order. Quality runs three checks side by side. Compatibility repeats the tests across three combinations of settings. Publish is skipped for snapshot versions. Deploy stops and waits for a person to approve it. These are the features that make a migration hard, so this is the behaviour to remember.

The pipeline needs two credentials, stored inside Jenkins. Here are both on the credentials page: a username and password, and a secret text. Jenkins masks the password. The names must match exactly what the pipeline script asks for. Both hold dummy values.

annotations.label: artifact-repo: username and password, used when publishing
inventory-deploy-token: secret text, used when deploying

scenes.narration: With the job created from the Jenkinsfile, with the script sandbox switched on, it shows on the dashboard. This screenshot was taken after both builds had run, so it already shows build number two as the latest.

annotations.label: Latest build, number two (taken after both builds)

scenes.source: README 1.4 (stages and Deploy gate); capture shots/04-stages-waiting.png (build 3, a repeat of the default build, caught while paused)
scenes.narration: Build number one uses the default settings. This is the Pipeline Overview, which draws the stages as a map. Quality fans out into three branches. Compatibility shows three matrix cells. To catch the pause on screen, this picture is the same default build run again, as build three. It has stopped at Deploy, waiting for approval.

data.title: Same default build, paused at Deploy

annotations.label: Compatibility: three matrix cells (names are cut off on screen)
The approval question waits here for a person

scenes.source: README 1.5; capture shots/05-input.png (build 3, while it waits)
scenes.narration: This is the approval page, captured while build three waits. It asks whether to deploy the release, and wants a change ticket, with a default of C H G zero zero zero zero. In this recording, builds one and three were approved through the API with the ticket C H G one two three four, not typed into this form.

annotations.label: Deploy approves it; Abort stops the build

scenes.source: hyperframes-walkthrough capture 000-walkthrough-60s/capture/jenkins (separate recording: build #1, SUCCESS, CHANGE_TICKET typed as CHG-1234, Deploy clicked); cuts as in docs/video/000-walkthrough-60s/edit.json, stages at 2x instead of 3x to fit the narration
scenes.narration: For comparison, here is the same pipeline filmed live, in a separate recording where it was build number one. The stages are sped up, and the speed is shown at the top. The build pauses at the Deploy gate. This time the same ticket is typed into the form, and Deploy is clicked. The build finishes successfully. The rest of this chapter returns to the builds approved through the API.
The console log records the approval: input requested, then approved by admin. The next lines deploy with the secret token masked, and write a small record holding the ticket and the approver.

annotations.label: Input requested, then approved by admin
The deploy token is masked in the log

scenes.source: README 1.6 Result and Artifacts; capture shots/06-build-page.png
scenes.narration: Build number one finished green. Its display name, version one point four to staging, was set by a script block in the pipeline. The page lists five build artifacts, and says it was approved by admin.

annotations.label: Green, with the name the pipeline set

scenes.narration: The Tests page shows twenty-one tests and no failures. Jenkins groups them into five packages: the unit tests, the integration test, and one set for each matrix cell.

annotations.label: Three matrix cells, five tests each

scenes.narration: Fingerprints are checksums that let Jenkins track a file across builds. The three files in the distribution folder are fingerprinted: the archive, its checksum file, and the build information.

annotations.label: Three files from the dist folder

beats.narration: The console log holds the key lines. A small helper downloads it, and this filter keeps four: the upload, which shows only the length of the password, the approval, the deploy, and the final success.

highlight.text: Password length shown, never the password

scenes.source: README 1.6 verification commands; capture verify-and-logs #0 to #5

beats.narration: Present is not the same as sound. So we download the four files the build archived, straight from Jenkins, in a temporary folder.
First, check the archive against the checksum file the pipeline recorded. The word O K means they match.
The build information file records the service, the version, the build name and the Python version used.
highlight: Version one point four point zero, build number one

beats.narration: The deploy record holds the change ticket we entered and the approver, taken from the approval. The walkthrough says GitHub Actions cannot reproduce these two values, so keep them in mind.

highlight.text: Ticket and approver came from the approval

beats.narration: Finally, unpack the archive and run the packaged tool. It reports two widgets and one gadget, with the right version.

scenes.narration: Build number two is a snapshot: version one point five, deploy environment none, integration tests switched off. There was no approval prompt. In the Pipeline Overview, Integration tests, Publish and Deploy are shown as skipped.

scenes.source: README 1.7 Console Output bullet; capture verify-and-logs #7
scenes.part: Part 1.7 · why the stages were skipped

beats.narration: The log gives the reasons. It announces the snapshot, then each of the three stages says it was skipped because its when condition was not met.

highlight.text: Three stages skipped, each says why

scenes.source: README 1.7 Tests, Build Artifacts; capture shots/17-b2-tests.png and 15-b2-build-page.png
scenes.narration: The Tests page now shows twenty tests, because the integration test did not run. The build also archived only the lint report, since nothing was packaged or published.
Back on the job page, the test trend drops from twenty-one to twenty, and both builds are listed. These are the two behaviours the converted workflow will later be compared against.

annotations.label: Latest artifacts: only the lint report

scenes.narration: To recap. We ran the example pipeline on a local Jenkins. Build one used the defaults, waited for approval, and produced a verified release. Build two, a snapshot, skipped three stages and ran twenty tests. That is the baseline. But this was one machine, one run of each case, with credentials and approval sent by script, and nothing here has been converted or run on GitHub yet.
